# Preface {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning}
**Draft.** This is an early, LLM-generated draft of the first three chapters, produced from an outline by Daniel Oberski. Everything in it — structure, examples, exercises, and claims — is provisional and subject to revision. The git history records what was written by the author and what was generated.
:::

This book is about a way of thinking, not a list of techniques.

Most statistics courses teach methods one at a time: here is the *t*-test, here is regression, here is ANOVA. Students then leave with a toolbox and no manual: which tool answers which question, and when should we believe the answer? This book starts from the other end. Every empirical study — whether it uses a *t*-test or a transformer — follows the same basic logic:

> A **research question** motivates a **design** for collecting data; the design makes a set of **assumptions** plausible; those assumptions define a **model**; and the results of fitting that model answer the research question — *to the extent that the assumptions hold*.

The chapters that follow work through this logic. We begin with the logic itself (@sec-rq-to-interpretation), then make it concrete by building statistical models directly from verbal theories (@sec-theory-to-glm), and then confront its limits: some questions simply cannot be answered by some designs, no matter how much data we collect (@sec-identification).

Each chapter is short and contains two kinds of exercises. *Inline exercises* appear throughout the text; they are meant to be done immediately, and you can reveal the answer directly below each one. *End-of-chapter exercises* are harder and are meant to test whether you can use the ideas, not just recognize them.

The practical exercises use R. If you prefer Python, everything here can be done there too; the ideas are what matter.
